podcast.body: This song is a World War II epic about the Dieppe Raid, an attack on the German-occupied port in France on August 19, 1942, where 4,000 people, mostly Canadian, died, were wounded, or captured, with nothing significant accomplished. The song emerged from one of Gord Downie's stream-of-consciousness live tangents and was performed on Saturday Night Live on March 27, 1997. "This is a song about the de-apparade, an attack on the German occupied port in France on August 19th, 1942. The 4,000 people died, were wounded or captured. Most of them were Canadian. And really nothing was accomplished. Many survivors of the attack died in the water while awaiting rescue. It really was a complete, nautical disaster."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song was born out of an extended jam session where new material was workshopped, a common practice for the band during their live performances, particularly within songs like "New Orleans is Sinking." "That's how nautical disaster and many other songs were born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song, released on the "Day for Night" album in 1994, originated from Gord Downie's improvisations during performances of "New Orleans is Sinking." It likely drew inspiration from historical events like the sinking of the Bismarck in 1941, which resulted in 2200 deaths, or from Captain Quint's account in the movie Jaws, detailing a ship sinking where 1100 men entered the water and only 316 survived. "That's one of the many hip songs that grew from Gord Downey's improvisations in the middle of performances of New Orleans' sinking."
